results.title: may also be of interest to consider variants of our Bayesian approach which treat the missing ratings differently. Referring to our approach as Bayes 1, a variant, Bayes 2, is obtained by treating values of \(x_{ij} = (x_{ij1}, \ldots, x_{ijR})\), for which item \(i\) was not rated by judge \(j\), as missing values in the likelihood (5). These missing values can be updated by introducing a Gibbs sampling step which samples from the full conditionals. Unfortunately, this dramatically increases the computational burden, especially if the data is sparse. Another variant, Bayes 3, is obtained by treating a missing rating as a new category, i.e. let \(x_{ij} = (x_{ij1}, \ldots, x_{ij(R+1)})\) and set \(x_{ij(R+1)} = 1\) if item \(i\) was not rated by judge \(j\). This approach, proposed by Breese et. al.(1998), requires renormalization of the posterior for prediction and appears to support larger values of \(G\). All these approaches are described more fully in Chien (1998). To compare these various approaches, we evaluated their predictive performance on the following three different datasets.
